{{Short description|Maxim about limits of scientific knowledge}}
{{italic title}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2017}}
[[File:Bois-Reymond.jpg|thumb|Emil du Bois-Reymond (1818–1896), promulgator of the maxim ''ignoramus et ignorabimus'' ([[Photogravure]] of a painting by [[Max Koner]])]]

The [[Latin]] maxim '''{{lang|la|ignoramus et ignorabimus}}''', meaning "we do not know and will not know", represents the idea that [[scientific knowledge]] is limited. It was popularized by [[Emil du Bois-Reymond]], a German [[physiologist]], in his 1872 address {{lang|de|italic=no|"Über die Grenzen des Naturerkennens"}} ("The Limits of Science").<ref>{{Cite book|last=du Bois-Reymond|first=Emil|title=Reden|publisher=Veit|year=1912|editor-last=du Bois-Reymond|editor-first=Estelle|volume=1|location=Leipzig|pages=441–473}}</ref>

== Seven "World Riddles" ==

[[Emil du Bois-Reymond]] first used the words {{lang|la|"ignoramus"}} and {{lang|la|"ignorabimus"}} at the close of his keynote address to the 1872 Congress of German Scientists and Physicians. As he saw it, science was bounded by two limits: the ultimate nature of matter and the enigma of consciousness. Eight years later, in a speech before the [[Prussian Academy of Sciences]], he expanded his list of conundrums to [[Emil du Bois-Reymond#On epistemology|seven "world riddles"]] or "shortcomings" of science.<ref>{{Cite book|last=du Bois-Reymond|first=Emil|title=Reden|publisher=Veit|year=1912|editor-last=du Bois-Reymond|editor-first=Estelle|volume=2|location=Leipzig|pages=65–98}}</ref> Three of these he declared to be "[[Transcendence (philosophy)#Kant (and modern philosophy)|transcendent]]", or permanently unknowable: "1. the ultimate nature of matter and energy, 2. the origin of motion, ... 5. the origin of simple [[Sense|sensations]]."<ref>{{cite journal |first=William E. Jr. |last=Leverette |title=E. L. Youmans' Crusade for Scientific Autonomy and Respectability |journal=American Quarterly |volume=17 |number=1 |date=Spring 1965 |page=21}}</ref>

== Hilbert's reaction ==

[[David Hilbert]], a widely respected German mathematician, suggested that such a conceptualization of human knowledge was too pessimistic, and that by considering questions unsolvable we limit our understanding.

In 1900, during an address to the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Paris, Hilbert suggested that answers to problems of mathematics are possible with human effort.  He declared, "in mathematics there is no {{lang|la|ignorabimus}}",<ref>{{Cite journal |first=David |last=Hilbert |title=Mathematical Problems: Lecture Delivered before the International Congress of Mathematicians at Paris in 1900 |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=8 |year=1902 |pages=437–79 |url=http://aleph0.clarku.edu/~djoyce/hilbert/problems.html | doi = 10.1090/S0002-9904-1902-00923-3 | mr = 1557926|doi-access=free }}</ref> and he worked with other [[Formalism (mathematics)|formalist]]s to establish [[foundations of mathematics#foundation crisis|foundations for mathematics]] during the early 20th century.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=McCarty|first=David C.|date=October 2005|title=Problems and riddles: Hilbert and the du Bois-Reymonds|journal=Synthese|language=en|volume=147|issue=1|pages=63–79|doi=10.1007/s11229-004-6207-5|s2cid=35716893|issn=0039-7857}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Reichenberger|first=Andrea|date=2019|title=From Solvability to Formal Decidability: Revisiting Hilbert's 'Non-Ignorabimus'|journal=Journal of Humanistic Mathematics |url=https://scholarship.claremont.edu/jhm/vol9/iss1/5|volume=9|issue=1|pages=49–80|doi=10.5642/jhummath.201901.05 |s2cid=127398451 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

On 8 September 1930, Hilbert elaborated his opinion in a celebrated address to the Society of German Scientists and Physicians, in [[Königsberg]]:<ref name=speech_hilbert_1930/>

{{blockquote|We must not believe those, who today, with philosophical bearing and deliberative tone, prophesy the fall of culture and accept the {{lang|la|ignorabimus}}. For us there is no {{lang|la|ignorabimus}}, and in my opinion none whatever in natural science. In opposition to the foolish {{lang|la|ignorabimus}} our slogan shall be {{lang|de|Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen}} ("We must know – we will know").<ref name=wissen/>|author=|title=|source=}}

Answers to some of [[Hilbert's 23 problems]] were found during the 20th century. Some have been answered definitively; some have not yet been solved; a few, most notably [[Continuum hypothesis|Cantor's continuum hypothesis]], have been shown to be undecidable on the basis of currently accepted principles.

In 1931, [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems]] showed that for any formal system of mathematics satisfying certain minimal requirements, there exist questions that cannot be answered within that system. While this does not exclude that the question can be answered unambiguously in another system, the incompleteness theorems are generally taken to imply that Hilbert's hopes for proving the consistency of mathematics using purely finitistic methods were unfounded.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reichenberger |first=Andrea |date=2019-01-31 |title=From Solvability to Formal Decidability: Revisiting Hilbert's "Non-Ignorabimus" |url=https://scholarship.claremont.edu/jhm/vol9/iss1/5 |journal=Journal of Humanistic Mathematics |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=49–80 |doi=10.5642/jhummath.201901.05 |issn=2159-8118|doi-access=free }}</ref> As this excludes the possibility of an absolute proof of consistency, there must always remain an ineliminable degree of insecurity about the foundations of mathematics: we will never be capable of knowing, once and for all, with a certainty unimpeachable even by the most stout skepticism, that there is no contradiction in our basic theories. (Note that this does not mean that such skepticism is rational; it only means that it cannot be refuted with absolute rigour.)

== Other responses ==
The [[sociologist]] [[Wolf Lepenies]] discussed the {{lang|la|Ignorabimus}} with the opinion that du Bois-Reymond was not really pessimistic about science:<ref>{{cite book|last=Lepenies|first=Wolf|author-link=Wolf Lepenies|title=Between Literature and Science: the Rise of Sociology|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge, UK|isbn=0-521-33810-7|page=272}}</ref>

{{blockquote|...&nbsp;it is in fact an incredibly self-confident support for scientific hubris masked as modesty&nbsp;...}}

This was in regards to [[Friedrich Wolters]], one of the members of the literary group "[[George-Kreis]]". Lepenies thought that Wolters misunderstood the degree of pessimism being expressed about science, but understood the implication that scientists themselves could be trusted with [[self-criticism]].

Lepenies was repeating the criticism, first leveled in 1874 by du Bois-Reymond's rival [[Ernst Haeckel]], that the "seemingly humble but actually presumptuous {{lang|la|Ignorabimus}} is the {{lang|la|Ignoratis}} of the infallible Vatican and of the 'Black International' which it heads."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Haeckel|first=Ernst|title=Anthropogenie, oder, Entwicklungsgeschichte des Menschen. Gemeinverständliche wissenschaftlich Vorträge über die Grundzüge der menschlichen Keimes- und Stammes-Geschichte|language=de|publisher=Wilhelm Engelmann|year=1874|isbn=3957384257|location=Leipzig|pages=xiii}}</ref> Haeckel overstated his charge: du Bois-Reymond had never supported the Catholic Church,<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Finkelstein |first=Gabriel |title=Emil du Bois-Reymond: Neuroscience, Self, and Society in Nineteenth-Century Germany |publisher=The MIT Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-1-4619-5032-5 |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts; London, England |pages=279–280 |oclc=864592470}}</ref> and far from professing humility he reminded his audience that while our knowledge was indeed bounded by mysteries of matter and mind, within these limits "the man of science is lord and master; he can analyze and synthesize, and no one can fathom the extent of his knowledge and power".<ref>{{Cite book|last=du Bois-Reymond|first=Emil|title=Reden|publisher=Veit|year=1912|editor-last=du Bois-Reymond|editor-first=Estelle|volume=1|location=Leipzig|pages=460}}</ref>

In response to his critics du Bois-Reymond modified his watchword in "The Seven World Riddles" (1880) to that of {{lang|la|"Dubitemus"}} ("We doubt it.")<ref>{{Cite book|last=du Bois-Reymond|first=Emil|title=Reden|publisher=Veit|year=1912|editor-last=du Bois-Reymond|editor-first=Estelle|volume=2|location=Leipzig|pages=83}}</ref>

[[William James]] referred to "Ignoramus, ignorabimus" in his lecture "Reflex Action and Theism" (1881) as an expression of [[agnosticism]], which gives man no practical tools for his volitions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Will to Believe |first=William |last=James |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/26659/26659-h/26659-h.htm#P129 |access-date=2022-04-11 |via=Project Gutenberg}}</ref> James had attended du Bois-Reymond's lectures in Berlin.<ref name=":0" />

The ''Quarterly Review'' also regarded the maxim as the ensign of agnosticism:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=[Hutton |first=Richard] |date=1895 |title=Professor Huxley's Creed |journal=Quarterly Review |volume=180 |issue=January |pages=160–188}}</ref><blockquote>To the average citizen who reads as he runs, and who is unacquainted with any tongue save his native British, it may well appear that the Gospel of Unbelief, preached among us during the last half-century, has had its four Evangelists–the Quadrilateral, as they have been called, whose works and outworks, demilunes and frowning bastions, take the public eye, while above them floats the agnostic banner with its strange device, "''Ignoramus et Ignorabimus''." </blockquote>The issue of whether science has limits continues to attract scholarly attention.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vidoni |first=Ferdinando |title=Ignorabimus!: Emil du Bois-Reymond und die Debatte über die Grenzen wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis im 19. Jahrhundert |publisher=Peter Lang |year=1991 |isbn=3-631-43339-5 |location=Frankfurt am Main |language=de |oclc=31070756}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tennant |first=Neil |date=2007-11-01 |title=Mind, mathematics and the Ignorabimusstreit |journal=British Journal for the History of Philosophy |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=745–773 |doi=10.1080/09608780701605036 |issn=0960-8788 |s2cid=145681301}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Der Ignorabimus-Streit |publisher=Felix Meiner |year=2012 |isbn=978-3-7873-2158-2 |editor-last=Bayertz |editor-first=Kurt |location=Hamburg |language=de |oclc=819620680 |editor-last2=Gerhard |editor-first2=Myriam |editor-last3=Jaeschke |editor-first3=Walter}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rescher |first=Nicholas |title=The limits of science |publisher=University of Pittsburgh Press |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-8229-7206-8 |edition=Revised |location=Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania |oclc=891385628}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Horgan |first1=John |title=The end of science: facing the limits of knowledge in the twilight of the scientific age |last2=Lenzo |first2=Jack |publisher=Basic Books |year=2015 |isbn=978-0-465-05085-7 |location=New York |oclc=905920357}}</ref>
